system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Alexander disease is an astrocytopathy caused predominantly by heterozygous gain-of-function variants in GFAP. Abnormal GFAP accumulation and astrocytic stress are associated with Rosenthal fibers and characteristic white-matter disease, often with frontal predominance in early-onset disease.
vignette: A 20-month-old boy is evaluated for progressive developmental delay, seizures, spasticity, and increasing head circumference. Brain MRI shows extensive bilateral frontal-predominant white-matter abnormalities. Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous pathogenic variant in GFAP.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Canavan disease is caused by ASPA deficiency with N-acetylaspartate accumulation; the GFAP variant points to Alexander disease.
Krabbe disease results from GALC deficiency and globoid-cell leukodystrophy rather than GFAP-associated astrocytopathy.
Metachromatic leukodystrophy is caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency with sulfatide accumulation.
X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is caused by ABCD1 defects with very-long-chain fatty-acid accumulation and does not explain a pathogenic GFAP variant.
key_expl: A pathogenic GFAP variant in a young child with macrocephaly, developmental regression/spasticity, seizures, and frontal-predominant white-matter disease is characteristic of Alexander disease. GFAP is the major intermediate filament of mature astrocytes; disease-causing variants act predominantly through gain of function and are associated with astrocytic Rosenthal fibers.
objective: Diagnose Alexander disease from its early neurologic phenotype, frontal-predominant white-matter involvement, and pathogenic GFAP variant.
